clinicalPearls: Phimosis is inability to retract the foreskin over the glans, and the crucial distinction is between the physiological non-retractility of childhood and true pathological scarring
Physiological phimosis reflects natural preputial adhesions and a non-scarred narrow tip that resolves spontaneously as the child grows, and needs only reassurance and hygiene advice
Pathological phimosis is characterised by a firm, white, cicatricial ring at the preputial opening, the hallmark of acquired scarring most often due to lichen sclerosus
Presenting features include a ballooning foreskin on voiding, recurrent balanitis, painful erections, bleeding fissures, and, in scarred cases, spraying or obstructed urinary stream
Forcible retraction of a physiological or inflamed foreskin should be avoided as it causes tears that heal with further scarring and can precipitate paraphimosis
A trial of topical corticosteroid can soften and resolve many non-scarred narrow foreskins and avoid surgery
True scarring phimosis, particularly from lichen sclerosus, typically requires circumcision, and excised tissue should be examined histologically
reference.pathophysiology: In the young child the foreskin is normally adherent to the glans and has a physiologically narrow opening; separation and retractility develop progressively over the early years, so non-retractility at this stage is developmental rather than diseased. Pathological phimosis instead results from acquired fibrosis of the distal prepuce. Chronic inflammation, most importantly lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans) but also recurrent balanoposthitis and the trauma of repeated forcible retraction, drives dermal scarring that contracts the preputial ring into a rigid, non-distensible band. This cicatricial narrowing prevents retraction, may obstruct the urinary stream, and can extend to involve the glans and meatus. Poorly controlled diabetes predisposes to the recurrent infection and inflammation that promote scarring.
additionalDifferentials: Paraphimosis, where a retracted foreskin cannot be reduced
Preputial adhesions or a congenitally short frenulum
Penile intraepithelial neoplasia or carcinoma presenting with preputial change
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination assessing retractility and looking for a cicatricial white ring
Inspection of the glans and meatus for coexisting lichen sclerosus or malignancy
Assessment of the urinary stream where obstruction or ballooning is reported
Blood glucose testing to detect diabetes predisposing to recurrent balanitis
Swab or microscopy if active infection is present
Histological examination of tissue removed at circumcision to confirm lichen sclerosus and exclude malignancy
redFlags: A firm white scarring ring or glans changes suggesting lichen sclerosus with its malignant association
A persistent ulcer or mass raising concern for penile carcinoma
Acute paraphimosis with a painful, swollen, irreducible retracted foreskin requiring urgent reduction
Obstructed voiding or urinary retention from severe narrowing
reference.prognosis: Physiological phimosis resolves spontaneously with growth, and many narrow non-scarred foreskins respond to topical steroid, whereas true scarring phimosis is effectively cured by circumcision, though associated lichen sclerosus of the glans or urethra may need continued attention.
pitfalls: Mislabelling normal developmental non-retractility as disease and recommending unnecessary surgery
Forcibly retracting the foreskin, causing tears, scarring, and paraphimosis
Missing underlying lichen sclerosus and its meatal, urethral, and malignant implications
Failing to send circumcision specimens for histology
Overlooking diabetes in a man with recurrent balanitis and secondary phimosis
references: British Association of Urological Surgeons guidance on circumcision
British Association of Dermatologists guidance on lichen sclerosus
management: Offer circumcision as the definitive treatment for the firm cicatricial preputial ring of true scarring phimosis
Trial a potent topical corticosteroid first for narrow but non-scarred foreskins, which may loosen the ring and avert surgery
Treat lichen sclerosus of the glans and prepuce with a potent topical corticosteroid
Treat active balanoposthitis with swab-directed topical or oral antimicrobials before elective surgery
Optimise glycaemic control in diabetes to reduce recurrent infection and refractory scarring
Avoid forcible retraction, which tears the foreskin and worsens scarring and can precipitate paraphimosis
Send excised preputial tissue for histology to confirm lichen sclerosus and exclude malignancy
Follow up for meatal or urethral stenosis and the long-term penile cancer risk associated with lichen sclerosus
